long.title: SpaceX's Wild Medical Cargo & PS5 On Xbox | Reality Shockwaves
long.pinned_comment: Would you rather see microgravity medical cures or physical soil samples returned from a Martian moon first? Let us know below!

intro.text: SpaceX is currently carrying lab-grown human brain tissue and artificial retinas into orbit, and number one could completely change how we treat degenerative disease.
We also have an Xbox running PlayStation code, an ultra-fast open-weight AI model, and Japan's daring mission to bring back pieces of a Martian moon.
Here are the top five major tech and science breakthroughs you need to see today.

scenes.text: Starting off at number five, advertising for a massive documentary about Elon Musk was abruptly shut down on social media.
The four-hour film, simply titled Musk, was directed by Oscar winner Alex Gibney and is currently rolling out into wider theatrical distribution.
According to The Hollywood Reporter, distributor Bleecker Street was notified that TikTok issued a permanent suspension on their advertising account, citing policies against political content.
This was not the only roadblock the documentary faced across major tech platforms.
Trailers were previously rejected by Meta and YouTube before both platforms reversed course, with Meta claiming the rejection was an error.
Musk's own platform, X, outright refused to carry any promotional ads for the release.
TikTok has now confirmed their suspension was also made in error and has restored the ad account.
While social platforms battle over content rules, reports say console modders just cracked open an entirely different software wall.
Coming in at number four, an Xbox Series X has officially run PlayStation 5 game code, but there is a major catch.
Developer Devran Cosmo Uenal managed to boot the PS5 edition of Quake Two directly on a Series X console using an Xbox controller.
He accomplished this using PS5X, an Xbox port of the open-source PC emulator compatibility layer called KytyPS5.
Both current-gen consoles share very similar AMD hardware, featuring eight Zen 2 cores, RDNA 2 graphics, and sixteen gigabytes of GDDR6 memory.
Because they use identical x86-64 processor architecture, the software acts like a translator rather than emulating an entire system from scratch.
However, the project relies on Xbox Developer Mode, where Microsoft's documentation caps games at just five gigabytes of memory.
That strict limitation unfortunately rules out the majority of current-gen PS5 titles under the current setup.
The developer also noted AI was involved in translating graphics to DirectX, describing it as an experimental research project.
Speaking of AI pushing technical boundaries, our next story reveals just how fast generative models are becoming.
At number three, DeepSeek has rolled out a new model called V4.1 Flash 1017 Max, and the raw speed numbers are turning heads.
According to benchmarks from Artificial Analysis, this new model clocks in at an astonishing 230 tokens per second.
To put that in perspective, the median speed for comparable open-weight models in its class sits at just 78 tokens per second.
The model features a massive one-million-token context window and handles both text and image inputs while generating text outputs.
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, it scored a 45, easily beating the category median score of 19.
It is also reasonably priced at thirty cents per million input tokens and one dollar and twenty cents per million output tokens.
The main tradeoff noted by evaluators is extreme verbosity, generating 210 million tokens during testing compared to the median of 140 million.
While machine intelligence is accelerating here on Earth, our next story involves sending robotic explorers all the way to Mars.
Taking the second spot today, Japan is preparing to launch one of the most daring planetary exploration attempts in history.
The Martian Moons eXploration mission, or MMX, is scheduled to launch aboard an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center.
If successful, MMX aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit with physical samples.
After a ten-month cruise to the Red Planet, the spacecraft will spend roughly three years conducting science around Mars' moon Phobos.
It carries a microwave-sized rover named IDEFIX, developed jointly by the French space agency CNES and Germany's DLR.
The craft will touch down directly on Phobos to scoop up surface material before making flybys of Deimos.
The sample return capsule is scheduled to leave Mars in late 2030, targeting a touchdown in Australia in 2031.
These samples could unlock secrets and shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago.
Our top story today is SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission, which just blasted off from Cape Canaveral on a Falcon 9 rocket.
The Dragon spacecraft is hauling over 6,300 pounds of vital hardware and science cargo to the International Space Station.
Among the most critical items aboard is the final pair of Roll-Out Solar Arrays, designed to augment the station's total electrical power.
NASA notes that extra electricity is necessary not just for running research, but also for eventually executing a safe, controlled deorbit of the station.
Even more exciting are the cutting-edge biotechnology payloads packed inside the pressurized capsule.
Researchers are sending hardware to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity, which could help restore vision for patients on Earth.
Dragon is also transporting three-dimensional heart tissue models to advance large-scale drug testing on future space missions.
Scientists have also included living brain organoids to analyze potential treatments for neurodegenerative illnesses like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
Dragon will stay docked through mid-November before splashing down off the coast of California with the completed experiments.

outro.text: From manufacturing artificial retinas in space to booting PlayStation games on Xbox hardware, tech is evolving at breakneck speed.
Which of these five breakthroughs do you think will have the biggest impact on our everyday lives?
Drop your thoughts in the comments below, hit subscribe, and we will see you tomorrow on Reality Shockwaves.
